solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Creature, rabbit, briefly seen by River Dee, perhaps (10)

indicatorNotes.briefly: a word said briefly is cut short, so NATTER loses its last letter
indicatorNotes.seen by: to be seen by something is to be beside it, so the pieces sit next to each other

blocks.note: to rabbit (on) is British slang for to chatter, NATTER, here without its last letter
R is the map abbreviation for river
the comedian Jack Dee is one Dee, so his first name stands in

annotation.surface: A nature-watcher spots a rabbit darting past on the banks of the River Dee.
annotation.walkthrough: 'River Dee' looks like one place, but the river is only R; this Dee is the British comedian Jack Dee.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the natterjack is a British toad, one kind of creature.

entries.clue: Ancient Greeks worshipped her near landing-place reportedly (4)

indicatorNotes.reportedly: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: nigh is an old word for near
a quay is a wharf where boats land, and it is pronounced 'key'
the two words run together as one two-syllable name

annotation.surface: Ancient worshippers visit a shrine down by the harbour.
annotation.walkthrough: NIGH plus QUAY, spoken, gives NIKE; the harbour setting hides that the landing-place is only there for its sound.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: Nike was the Greek goddess of victory, worshipped across ancient Greece.

entries.clue: Elevated shot, notice tennis players will use it (7)

indicatorNotes.Elevated: in a down clue, lifting the letters up means reading them from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: a nip is a small shot of spirits
to spot something is to notice it

annotation.surface: A tennis coach explains a lofted shot, pinning up a notice for the players.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Elevated shot' looks like a lob on court, but 'shot' is a drink. 'Elevated' only works as a turnaround because this is a down clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: topspin is the forward rotation tennis players put on the ball.

entries.clue: Engineer, i.e. MSc, working as secret influential adviser (8,5)

indicatorNotes.working: letters that are working are being put to use and moved about, so they change order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters; 'i.e.' and 'MSc' are just their letters

annotation.surface: An engineer with a master's degree quietly steers the boss's decisions.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' reads as a job title or a verb meaning to contrive, but it is only letters. The phrase is French for 'grey eminence', first used of Cardinal Richelieu's adviser.
annotation.definitionFit: A borrowed phrase: an éminence grise is someone who wields power unofficially from behind the scenes.

entries.clue: Day after rock star almost gets nicked (6)

indicatorNotes.almost: almost the whole name, so it stops one letter short
indicatorNotes.after: D for day follows the shortened rock star in the answer

blocks.note: Mick Jagger of the Rolling Stones, without his final R
D is the standard abbreviation for day

annotation.surface: A rock star is arrested the day after a gig.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gets nicked' is British slang for gets arrested, which the surface leans on; the definition uses 'nicked' in its other sense, notched.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in a second sense: an edge covered in small nicks is notched and uneven.

entries.clue: Somewhere revel carousing around, keeping comparatively smart (8)

indicatorNotes.keeping: the words keep the answer inside them, running across their boundaries
indicatorNotes.around: the kept letters are turned around, so they are read right to left

blocks.note: the last two letters of the first word, all of the second, and the first letter of the third, read from right to left

annotation.surface: Partygoers carouse somewhere, and one of them keeps a bit sharper than the rest.
annotation.walkthrough: somewhe(RE REVEL C)arousing, read backwards, gives C-LEVER-ERE. The run crosses three words, so reading forwards will not find it.
annotation.definitionFit: A comparative adjective: 'smart' and 'clever' are synonyms, and 'comparatively' asks for the -er form.

entries.clue: Taking coat from stylish young woman (4)

indicatorNotes.Taking coat from: a coat is the outer layer, so taking it off strips the first and last letters

blocks.note: classy means stylish; lose the outer C and Y

annotation.surface: Someone helps a fashionable young woman off with her coat.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes the coat a garment; here it is the word's outer letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional synonym: lass is the Scottish and northern English word for a girl or young woman.

entries.clue: Titular Shakespeare role, male last to die maybe (7)

indicatorNotes.last: 'last' places M at the very end, after the Shakespeare role

blocks.note: Mark Antony is named in the title of Antony and Cleopatra
M is the standard abbreviation for male

annotation.surface: An actor playing Shakespeare's title hero is the last man to die on stage.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Last to die' reads as a death scene, but 'last' only places M, and 'die maybe' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: 'die' is the opposite of 'live', so it is one instance of an antonym.

entries.clue: Boy racer, possibly amphetamine addict (10)

blocks.note: a boy racer is British slang for a young man who drives fast, flashy cars
'speed' is street slang for amphetamine

annotation.surface: A young tearaway driver turns out to be hooked on pills.
annotation.walkthrough: The two senses share one phrase: an obsession with going fast, and a habit named after the drug's nickname.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are informal: one lives for fast driving, the other is dependent on the drug called speed.

entries.clue: Writer, man Hislop regularly is cutting about (7)

indicatorNotes.regularly: at regular intervals, so every second letter is taken
indicatorNotes.about: turned about, the chosen letters face the other way
indicatorNotes.is cutting: the letters cut into the man, splitting him in two

blocks.note: a king is one of the men on a chessboard
h(I)s(L)o(P), the even letters

annotation.surface: The satirist Ian Hislop takes his pen to a rival writer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Man' as a chess piece is a common crossword device. Ian Hislop edits the British satirical magazine Private Eye.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Rudyard Kipling, author of The Jungle Book, is one writer.

entries.clue: Style improvement, it lengthened pockets (7)

indicatorNotes.pockets: to pocket something is to hold it inside, as these words hold the answer

blocks.note: the last three letters of the first word, all of the second, and the first two of the third

annotation.surface: A tailor improves a jacket by lengthening its pockets.
annotation.walkthrough: improvem(ENT IT LE)ngthened. 'Style' sits at the start like a fashion word, but it is a verb: to style someone is to call them by a title.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to style someone 'Sir' is to give them that title.

entries.clue: Slow, as in late to make latte, say? (4-9)

blocks.note: the surface pushes a barista running late with a coffee

blocks.clueFragment: as in late to make latte, say?
blocks.note: the setter means spelling: LATE must swallow a T, the abbreviation for time, to become LATTE

annotation.surface: A barista is running late with a coffee order.
annotation.walkthrough: A word that eats a T is, read literally, time-consuming, since T is short for time. That second reading backs up the plain definition 'Slow'.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a time-consuming job takes a long time, so it is slow.

entries.clue: Fixed earlier, printer deemed to be broken (13)

indicatorNotes.to be broken: something broken falls apart, and its pieces can be put back in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: A printer that was repaired earlier is now declared broken again.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fixed' in the surface sounds like repaired; the definition uses its other sense, settled.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something predetermined was settled, fixed, in advance.

entries.clue: Succeeded boarding ship mines damaged, creating mischief (10)

indicatorNotes.boarding: to board a ship is to go inside it, so S goes in among the other letters
indicatorNotes.damaged: damaged letters are knocked out of shape, into a new order

blocks.note: S for succeeded, as in lists of monarchs
anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: A boarding party damages a ship's mines, causing havoc.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boarding ship' looks like a naval raid; it only tells S to go inside the rearranged letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: impishness is playful naughtiness, the spirit of mischief.

entries.clue: Current champ tours Olympic city (6)

indicatorNotes.tours: to tour a place is to travel all round it, so MUNCH goes round I

blocks.note: to champ is to chew noisily
I is the physics symbol for electric current

annotation.surface: The reigning champion takes a tour of a city that has hosted the Olympics.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Current champ' reads as the title holder, but 'champ' is the verb to chew.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this German city hosted the 1972 Summer Olympics.

entries.clue: Former Wimbledon champion (not British) essentially encouraging novice (8)

indicatorNotes.not: the bracketed 'not British' tells us the B is left out
indicatorNotes.essentially: the essence of a word is its core, the middle letter

blocks.note: John Newcombe, the Australian who won Wimbledon three times, minus B for British
the sixth of eleven letters, the middle of encouRaging

annotation.surface: A retired Wimbledon champion from abroad encourages a beginner.
annotation.walkthrough: The brackets read as an aside about his nationality, which is true of Newcombe, but they are the instruction to delete.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a newcomer is someone new to an activity, a novice.

entries.clue: German condemned probing newspaper piece (8)

indicatorNotes.condemned: a condemned building is fit only to be pulled down, so the word's letters are rebuilt
indicatorNotes.probing: a probe goes in, so the letters go into the newspaper

blocks.note: FT is the Financial Times
GERMAN rearranged

annotation.surface: A German journalist is condemned for a probing newspaper piece.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Newspaper piece' looks like one phrase, an article, but 'piece' stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a fragment is a small piece broken off something.

entries.clue: Obtain survey Neil oddly defends, rounding numbers (8)

indicatorNotes.oddly: oddly means in the odd positions: first, third, fifth letters
indicatorNotes.defends: defenders surround what they protect, so these letters go round GET
indicatorNotes.rounding: to round is to turn back, so everything is read backwards

blocks.note: (S)u(R)v(E)y (N)e(I)l, the odd letters across both words
to get is to obtain

annotation.surface: Someone wants a survey that Neil defends by rounding off its figures.
annotation.walkthrough: SRE and NI go round GET, and the whole reads backwards. 'Rounding numbers' reads as arithmetic, but 'numbers' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: integers are whole numbers, one class of number.

entries.clue: Expression about Harry’s weight (7)

indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so the expression wraps around the next word

blocks.note: tone of voice is a person's expression
to harry someone is to pester or nag them

annotation.surface: A comment is made about Prince Harry's weight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Harry' looks like a name but is the verb to pester.
annotation.definitionFit: A specialist sense: tonnage is weight measured in tons, especially of ships or cargo.

entries.clue: In the morning, energy drink will stop flipping problem (6)

indicatorNotes.flipping: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: AM, ante meridiem, means in the morning
gin, the spirit
E is the physics symbol for energy

annotation.surface: A morning energy drink is supposed to put a stop to some nagging trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping problem' reads as a mild British curse, like 'blooming problem'; here 'flipping' turns the letters back to front.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an enigma is a puzzle, a problem hard to solve.

entries.clue: Choose KLM for flights and share costs equally (2,5)

blocks.note: KLM is the national airline of the Netherlands, so this reads literally as travelling the Dutch way
an idiom for everyone paying their own part of the bill

annotation.surface: Friends pick the Dutch airline for a trip and split the fares.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half is cryptic: 'go' is taken literally, flying with the Dutch airline.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom in both halves: to go Dutch is to split a bill, and literally to travel Dutch.

entries.clue: Dumping married rock singer (6)

indicatorNotes.Dumping: to dump something is to throw it out, so the M is removed

blocks.note: to rock is to shake or tremble
M for married, as on forms; it is taken out

annotation.surface: A rock singer ditches his wife.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rock singer' looks like one musician; 'rock' is the verb to shake.
annotation.definitionFit: A specialist sense: a treble is a boy who sings the highest part in a choir.

entries.clue: Where one might shoot, which could suggest thin gun? (7-6)

blocks.note: the surface pushes a firing range and a flimsy weapon
the setter means a reverse clue: grind up the first word of the answer and you get the letters THIN GUN

annotation.surface: A shooter looks for a good spot, worried that the gun looks flimsy.
annotation.walkthrough: HUNTING is an anagram of THIN GUN, and 'ground' is a fair anagram signal, so the answer is itself an instruction that produces the clue's words.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: a hunting ground is land where game is shot.

entries.clue: Smirk of embarrassment when spilling tea (4)

indicatorNotes.when spilling: spilt tea runs out of the cup, so CHA runs out of the word

blocks.note: chagrin is embarrassed annoyance
cha is British slang for tea, from Chinese; it is taken out

annotation.surface: Someone smirks awkwardly after knocking over the tea.
annotation.walkthrough: The embarrassment in the surface is the word being cut, not the reason for the smirk.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: a smirk is a smug, knowing kind of smile.

entries.clue: Stand before door that revolves (7)

indicatorNotes.that revolves: something that revolves turns round, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: ere is an old word for before
a gate is an outdoor door

annotation.surface: Someone waits in front of a revolving door.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stand' looks like a verb, as in standing at a door; it is the noun, a piece of furniture.
annotation.definitionFit: A specialist word from French: an étagère is a stand of open shelves for displaying ornaments.

entries.clue: Attack famous surgeon behind back of pub (7)

indicatorNotes.back of: the back of a word is its final letter
indicatorNotes.behind: to stand behind something is to come after it, so the surgeon follows B

blocks.note: the last letter of pub
Joseph Lister, the British pioneer of antiseptic surgery

annotation.surface: A well-known surgeon is set upon behind a pub.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Attack' reads as a physical assault; the answer is the verb for scalding criticism.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: to blister someone is to attack them with criticism harsh enough to burn.

entries.clue: Drop something in the garden? (4)

blocks.note: a verb: trees let their leaves fall this way
a noun: the wooden hut where tools are kept

annotation.surface: A gardener lets something fall among the plants.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark invites reading the clue as one garden scene, with trees dropping leaves.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: to cast off, as leaves or skin, and a small outbuilding.

entries.clue: Support son facing awkward tenth green, one birdie ultimately missed (10)

indicatorNotes.facing: to face something is to stand in front of it, so S comes first
indicatorNotes.awkward: awkward letters sit in an awkward, jumbled order
indicatorNotes.ultimately: ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter of birdie is used
indicatorNotes.missed: something missed is left out, so that E drops from the fodder

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
anagram fodder before one letter is removed
the last letter of birdie; one of the three Es in the fodder goes

annotation.surface: A golfer's son helps on a tricky tenth green after missing a birdie putt.
annotation.walkthrough: The golf words are misdirection: a birdie is one under par on a hole, but here it only supplies its final E.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to support a wall or a case is to make it stronger.
